#### About Dante Alighieri

Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) was the Florentine poet-philosopher of the Divine Comedy, exiled in the Guelf–Ghibelline conflicts. He wrote vernacular epic that synthesizes Aristotelian ethics, scholastic theology, and civic passion.

### Interpretation

Dante closes the Paradiso with this, and the grammar matters: love is the subject and the celestial machinery is what it moves. The claim is that the order of the cosmos is not a mechanism but an attraction, so the whole structure holds because of what draws it rather than what pushes it. Arriving here at the end of the poem, the sentence is the resolution of the journey rather than a proposition in it.

#### Why it matters

It offers a different image of order — one that coheres by being drawn rather than by being driven, which changes what holds a thing together.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “the Love that moves the sun and the…”?

“the Love that moves the sun and the…” comes from Paradiso, XXXIII.145, attributed to Dante Alighieri.

#### What does Dante Alighieri mean by love?

Greek distinctions among eros, philia, and agape, Confucian relational ethics, and modern debates about romantic love keep the theme philosophically precise rather than merely sentimental. This passage enters that discussion through love, nature, order.
